title: Sorry Is Not a Text
part: PART FOUR: THE OTHER KIND OF CONFIDENCE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #43: Say you're sorry in a text.*

The phone screen glows, bright and accusatory. I type: *I am so sorry Priya I was a jerk because I was having a nervous breakdown.* I delete it. I type: *My bad.* I delete that. It sounds like a guy who just crashed his car into a fence. I stare at the blinking cursor, a tiny digital heartbeat judging me.

I grab the bag Ollie left on my desk. He gave me two bags of orange slices, which is suspiciously generous for a kid who usually hoards them. "For the apology," he had said, grinning with his mouth full. "They help with the talking."

I put on my cleats. The left lace is green, the right is orange. They match my mood, which is currently a tangled knot. I ride my bike to Priya’s house, the wind hitting my face like a cold, honest slap. The street is quiet. Her yellow windbreaker hangs on the porch hook, empty.

I knock. The door opens. It is not Priya. It is her mother, who looks at me with eyes that see everything, including the orange slices in my hand and the fact that I have nowhere to be.

"Go to the back," she says, stepping aside. "She is in the yard."
pages.image: A wiry girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband bikes down a suburban street, holding a bag of orange slices, looking anxious; a yellow windbreaker hangs on a porch hook in the background.

pages.text:
Priya is in the backyard, throwing a tennis ball against the garage door. *Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch.* Her eyes are wide open, which is a new development, because usually the ball is a scary moving object and her eyes are closed, praying for a miracle.

I stand by the fence, feeling like I am about to confess a crime I haven’t committed yet.

"Priya," I say.

She stops. The ball hangs in her oversized glove, looking like a tiny orange planet in a white orbit. She turns, her glasses sliding down her nose.

"I said something mean," I start, then stop. My throat feels like it is filled with gravel. "I said you were the reason we lost. And I said you should have caught that ball."

I take a breath. The air tastes like autumn and regret.

"I was scared," I say, my voice coming out smaller than I want it to. "I was scared of losing again. And I took it out on you. It was about me, not you. I am sorry."

I don’t wait for a speech. I just stand there, hands in my pockets, waiting to be yelled at or ignored. The silence stretches, thin and taut.
pages.image: Two girls stand in a backyard; one tiny girl with glasses and oversized gloves holds a tennis ball, while the other girl with a ponytail stands by a wooden fence, looking down at the grass.

pages.text:
Priya stares at the dirt, kicking a pebble into the soil with her cleat.

"I knew you were scared," she says, her voice steady despite the silence between us. "You always get loud when you're afraid, like a car engine revving too high in a school parking lot."

I don't have a response for that specific comparison, so I just nod, feeling the gravel in my throat settle.

"You were right about the goals," she continues, pulling one of her oversized gloves off. "We let too many in. I should be better. I know I should be better." She looks up, her eyes sharp and clear behind her sports band. "But you were wrong about who they belonged to. They aren't just my failures. They are ours."

She tucks the glove under her arm. "My true thing isn't just angles. It is this: Even when I let one in, I stay."

My legs give out, so I sit down on the grass, the cool dampness seeping through my shorts and chilling my skin. Priya sits next to me, close enough that our shoulders touch and I can feel the warmth of her jersey.

"I stayed," she says, looking at the fence. "Because of the team. And because of you, Dani. Even when you were being a mess."
pages.image: Two girls sit side by side on green grass in a backyard; the taller girl has her head in her hands, while the smaller girl rests a hand on her shoulder; a tennis ball lies on the lawn nearby.

pages.text:
We sit there for a minute, breathing the same air. Then Priya picks up the tennis ball.

"Watch," she says.

She throws it at the garage door, but not straight. She angles it so it bounces off the siding and comes back to her hand. Then she throws it at a slant, hitting the corner of the door. It ricochets perfectly into her glove.

"It’s a map," she says. "The field is not just grass. It is a map of slopes and angles. The ball wants to go certain ways. We just have to tell it where."

I pull out my red notebook. For the first time, I don't write a way to lose. I draw an arrow. Then another. Priya leans over, her hair brushing my arm, and adds a little note in the corner of the page.

It is not a loss anymore. It is a strategy.
pages.image: An open notebook with a red cover lying on the grass, its pages full of hand-drawn soccer goal diagrams with arrows and dotted lines, a pair of big goalkeeper gloves resting beside it, a girl's hand pointing at a diagram

pages.text:
My phone buzzes in my pocket, but I ignore it completely. Instead, I hear the low, steady rumble of my dad’s truck idling in the driveway, a sound that usually means he’s been waiting. Through the kitchen window, I can see his silhouette against the gray morning light. He’s still wearing his mechanic’s shirt, one hand resting on the wheel while he waits for me to finish my thoughts.

I climb into the passenger seat, and the familiar scent of motor oil and stale coffee immediately wraps around me. It smells like the inside of a garage on a hot day, thick and warm.

"Dad," I say, my voice sounding smaller than I want it to. "I have been afraid for a long time."

He turns to look at me. His eyes are tired, dark circles under them, but they are steady and calm.

"That people only like me when I win," I finish, the words sticking in my throat. "That I am only good when the scoreboard says so."

He grips the steering wheel, and his knuckles turn white against the plastic. For a second, he says nothing, just watching the road ahead. Then he exhales, a long, rough sound that rumbles through the cab.

"I liked you when you were three," he says finally. "You couldn't kick a ball. You kicked your own shoe. I still do."

He doesn't say anything else. He puts the truck in gear, and the engine hums to life. It is exactly enough.
pages.image: Dani, a girl with a ponytail, sits in the passenger seat of her dad's pickup truck looking out the window with a calm expression; her dad, a big man in a mechanic's work shirt, drives with both hands on the wheel
